traveler: Parzival (Parzival von Waleis, son of Gahmuret of Anjou and Herzeloyde of Waleis)
title: Wolfram's Parzival: Soltane to the Grail Throne
years: 826-848 (Werner Greub's chronology: Wolfram's Parzival read as ninth-century history)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Kanvoleis and Soltane: The Boy in the Waste Forest

stops.name: Kanvoleis (Colmar), the tournament of the Leoplane
stops.campa: Gahmuret rides in from Doled across the Bourgondian road and enters Kanvoleis by the lower gate, past Herzeloyde's own royal court at the town's old Königshof. On the meadow called Leoplane, beyond the pontoon bridge over the Rhine's Alsatian arm, the tournament for the queen's hand is proclaimed. Knights of a hundred lands break their lances on the green until Gahmuret alone stands unhorsed by no man. Herzeloyde descends and crowns him. Within the month he is her husband, though the sea and the Baruc's wars still call his restless heart away.
suggested_refs: Musée d'Unterlinden, Colmar, built on the site of Herzeloyde's lower Königshof, per Werner Greub's identification
The Route d'Ingersheim, traditional line of the old pontoon-bridge to the Leoplane
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book II, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 13, 'Anschouwe and Kanvoleis'

stops.name: Kanvoleis (Colmar), the birth and the widowing
stops.campa: Gahmuret rides east to serve the Baruc of Baghdad and falls beneath its walls, his death told by a bloodied shirt laid before the queen. Within the year, in mourning at Kanvoleis, Herzeloyde bears a son. She names him Parzival, right-through-the-middle, for the grief that has ridden straight through her own heart, and holds him to her breast murmuring the words a mother gives a child she means to keep from the world. She resolves he shall never hear the word knight, and gathers her household to flee the court entire into the deep forest of Soltane.
stops.quote: Bon fils, Cher fils, Beau fils.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book II, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Herzeloyde to her newborn son
suggested_refs: The Isenheim Altarpiece panels by Grünewald, housed in the former lower Königshof, now the Musée d'Unterlinden
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book II
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 13

stops.name: Soltane Forest, Rengersmatt, the boy and the birds
stops.campa: At the clearing called Rengersmatt, deep in the Soltane wood above Arlesheim, Herzeloyde raises her son among farmhands and oxen, letting him know no weapon but the little bow he cuts himself, no world but forest and stream. One bright morning he weeps to hear the birds fall silent under his mother's snares, set because their song stirs in him a longing she cannot bear. Are they God's creatures, she tells him, gentling her wrath; he presses her further, wide-eyed: Mother, who is God? She answers as best a mother can, and does not know she has planted the whole quest in a single question.
stops.quote: Then the boy spake, 'Now sweet my mother, why trouble the birds so sore? Forsooth they can ne'er have harmed thee, ah, leave them in peace once more!'
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: Rengersmatt farmhouse, Schönmattweg, Arlesheim, identified by Werner Greub as the site of Herzeloyde's estate
The Ermitage Arlesheim landscape garden, whose grounds Greub reads as the whole of Soltane Forest
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12, 'Terre de salvaesche'

stops.name: Winterhalde, the long slope where he met the knights
stops.campa: On the long mountain slope above Rengersmatt, where the road from Basle drops toward Münchenstein, four knights in shining mail come pounding through in pursuit of an abductor. The boy of fourteen, dazzled by the sun on their armor, falls to his knees, certain he has seen God as his mother described Him: brighter than the day. Their lord laughs him gently upright and tells him he is no god but a knight, and that a boy so goodly should ride for King Arthur's court to be made one. Parzival runs home shouting the word that will end his mother's peace forever.
stops.quote: I met in the woods, sweet mother, four men I deemed gods indeed, so light were they all and shining, God Himself ne'er could brighter be, and of knighthood they spake, and King Arthur, who might well make a knight of me!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: Winterhalde, the slope above Münchenstein still bearing that name, identified by Werner Greub as the site of the encounter
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: Soltane, the fool's garb, the farewell, and Herzeloyde's death
stops.campa: Unable to hold him, Herzeloyde dresses her son in a fool's motley of sackcloth, hoping ridicule will turn him back before the world can harm him, and gives him her whole store of counsel in one night: avoid untrodden paths, do not ford the dark water, greet every stranger fairly, heed a grey-headed man's advice, and take gladly whatever ring or kiss a lady offers. At dawn she kisses him and sends him from the gate. She watches him out of sight, falls to the ground, and by the grief of that single hour, not many days after, she is dead.
stops.quote: Keep thou ever from paths untrodden and ford not the darkling stream, where the waters flow clear and limpid, there safe is the ford I ween... And one thing, my son, would I tell thee: canst thou win from a maid her ring and her greeting fair, thou shalt take them, and sorrow hath lost her sting!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Herzeloyde's counsel
suggested_refs: The Soltane clearing behind the Ermitage, traditional site of Herzeloyde's farewell and death
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: Bromhübel, the tent of the sleeping Jeschute
stops.campa: A day and a night the boy wanders Brizljan Forest along the dark, swollen Dorfbach, refusing by his mother's word to ford it, until at last, at Bromhübel, he crosses at a shallow ford and finds a rich tent pitched in a green meadow. Within, Duchess Jeschute lies asleep. Remembering only take the ring, take the kiss, he presses his mouth to hers, wrestles the ring from her hand and the brooch from her breast, and eats her provisions before riding on, well pleased with himself, wholly unaware he has just ruined a marriage and doomed a knight to death by his silence.
stops.quote: Then she spake in her fear and anguish, 'Twas a fool, he who came to me, and yet tho' a fool, of all men I wot he may fairest be!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Jeschute to Duke Orilus
suggested_refs: Bromhübel, Arlesheim, identified by Werner Greub as the site of Jeschute's tent
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: Holleberg, lost on the road to Karminal, and Sigune among the rocks
stops.campa: He rides for Arthur's hunting lodge Karminal, following the Holleberg south, but fails to hold the ridge and loses the track entirely, circling back by evening to the rock arch at the edge of Soltane Forest. There, on a fallen linden, sits Sigune, cradling in her lap the embalmed body of Schionatulander, her betrothed, slain that same day by jealous Orilus. She names him for the first time, Parzival, right-through-the-middle, telling him his own lineage before he knows it himself, and points him at last, correctly, toward Nantua and the court he seeks.
suggested_refs: The rock arch and Fontane la salvaesche at the Ermitage Arlesheim, identified as the site of this first Sigune scene by Rudolf Steiner in 1913 and confirmed geographically by Werner Greub
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12
Emil Bock, Rudolf Steiner (on Steiner's 1913 identification)

stops.name: The headwaters of the Birs, the smooth-trodden road
stops.campa: Sigune, fearing he will blunder into Orilus's own country at Landskron, sends him instead the long way, up the Birs to its source in the Jura folds and over the height of land into the headwaters of the Ain, a road smooth-trodden and wide, safely clear of the man whose wife he unwittingly robbed. He rides single-mindedly, hardly resting, through country he has never seen, forest giving way to limestone gorge and gorge to open upland, carrying nothing of the world but a fool's coat, a stolen ring, and a name he has only just learned is his own.
suggested_refs: The Jura watershed between the Birs and Ain river systems, Werner Greub's proposed route
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 11, 'Bertane, the Land of King Arthur'

stops.name: Cluse (Montréal-la-Cluse), the first sight of Nantua
stops.campa: A fisherman, the last stranger Parzival greets on the road, brings him down through the narrow cluse in the Jura fold to a place from which, across a meadow not too broad, the roofs and towers of Nantua first come into view, cupped in its lake at the bottom of the gorge. This is the gate to the land of Bertane, and Parzival, half from the fisherman's word and half from his own wild joy, understands he is close now to the thing he has ridden toward without knowing its shape: a king, a table, a knighthood not yet his.
suggested_refs: The pass at Montréal-la-Cluse, below Nantua, identified by Werner Greub with Wolfram's Muntane Cluse
sources: Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 11

stops.name: Nantua (Nantes), the death of Ither and the making of the Red Knight
stops.campa: At Arthur's court by the lake, Ither, the Red Knight, sits his charger outside the gate demanding satisfaction for a wrong; a page's spilled wine has already struck Cunneware into laughter for the first time in years at the sight of the fool who will avenge her. Parzival, refused a horse and arms by any knight of sense, rides straight at Ither and puts his javelin through the gap between helm and visor. Ither falls dead in his own red armor; Parzival strips it from him, refuses his own fool's coat, and rides from Nantua no longer a boy but the Red Knight.
stops.quote: Then Parzival sprang up swiftly and stood wrathful upon his feet, and he grasped his javelin firmly... and thro' eye and neck it struck him, and the knight on the plain lay dead.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: The Tour de la Late, ninth-century remains at Nantua identified by Werner Greub as part of Arthur's headquarters
The moraine lake of Nantua, whose ninth-century shoreline reached further than today's
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 11

stops.name: Graharz (Grenoble), the counsel of Gurnemanz
stops.campa: In Graisivaudan below Grenoble, Parzival finds the grey-headed lord his mother foretold, Gurnemanz, kin to his uncle Kyot, and submits at last to be taught: how to sit a horse, how to spare a beaten foe, how to keep his harness clean. Above all Gurnemanz warns him against a fault the boy does not yet know he has: ask no question so freely that it shames the one who answers it, yet never withhold a fitting answer of your own. Parzival receives the words like all his mother's counsel, whole, unexamined, and will carry them, misapplied, to the one door in the world where silence is the sin.
stops.quote: 'Nor be thou so swift to question, yet I would not that thou withhold an answer good and fitting to the speech one with thee would hold.'
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Gurnemanz's counsel
suggested_refs: Graisivaudan valley below Grenoble, identified with Wolfram's Graswaldan by prior Wolfram scholarship and confirmed by Werner Greub
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 11

stops.name: Graharz (Grenoble), the parting and Liaze unspoken
stops.campa: Twice seven days Parzival dwells in Gurnemanz's household, long enough to fall wordlessly in love with Liassé, the old lord's daughter, and to be offered, if he will only stay, her hand and the whole inheritance of Graharz. He will not take what he has not yet earned. Hearing how three sons of this house died in arms, he promises instead to come back and claim her on the day he has won knightly fame worth the asking, and rides on toward Pelrapeire still a novice; and the prince, who has already lost thrice at sorrow's game, must now count his loss fourfold.
stops.quote: Little wisdom have I, yet if ever the day I know when I win knightly fame and honour, so that maiden I well may woo, thou shalt give unto me Liassé, thy daughter so fair and true.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Parzival to Gurnemanz at the parting
suggested_refs: Graisivaudan valley, traditional site of Gurnemanz's household
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 11

segments.name: Pelrapeire: The Liberation and the Marriage

stops.name: Pelrapeire (Montpellier), the starving city
stops.campa: Riding the road from Graharz, Parzival comes on Pelrapeire under siege, its granaries emptied, its young queen Condwiramurs pressed by an unwanted suitor, Clamide, whose seneschal Kingrun has starved the town toward surrender. The gate opens to the unknown Red Knight more from desperation than hope. Condwiramurs herself, though a queen ruling alone, comes to his chamber that first night only to weep and ask his help, and lies beside him chastely till dawn, for Parzival, new to love as to everything else, does not yet know what more a wife might ask of a husband.
suggested_refs: Montpellieret, the quarter of Montpellier identified by Werner Greub with Wolfram's Pelrapeire and Willehalm's Komarzi
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IV
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, part I, 'Kyot-Willehalm'

stops.name: Pelrapeire, the duels with Kingrun and Clamide
stops.campa: Parzival rides out and unhorses the seneschal Kingrun in single combat, then, when Clamide himself arrives with his army, defeats the king as well, in each case sparing the beaten man's life exactly as Gurnemanz taught him and sending him instead to surrender himself at Arthur's court in Bertane. The besieging host, leaderless, withdraws. Pelrapeire's granaries fill again from the countryside; the city that had been eating its last stores now feasts its deliverer, and Condwiramurs, who has watched her fate decided twice in a single day by a boy barely a knight, begins for the first time to hope.
suggested_refs: The old ramparts of Montpellieret, traditional site of the siege
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IV
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 11 (on Kingrun and Clamide's route to Arthur via Lyon)

stops.name: Pelrapeire, the marriage of Condwiramurs
stops.campa: With the siege broken, Condwiramurs and Parzival marry, and here too he learns from Kyot, Willehalm of Toulouse and Orange retired to his hunting lodge at Le Verdus, uncle to the queen and to Parzival's own dead mother's line, the man who found the Grail family in the forest behind Arlesheim twenty years before and married its first bearer, Schoysiane. Under Kyot's tutelage and his wife's rule Parzival passes more than a year at Pelrapeire, a husband and a king by marriage, still ignorant that the greatest test of his life, and his family's, waits a few months' ride to the north.
suggested_refs: Le Verdus hunting lodge near Saint-Guilhelm-le-Désert, Kyot-Willehalm's retirement seat per Werner Greub
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IV
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, part I, 'Kyot-Willehalm'

stops.name: Pelrapeire, the departure in search of his mother
stops.campa: Word of Herzeloyde's death has never reached her son. Restless after more than a year of settled rule, and troubled by a wish to know how his mother fares, Parzival asks his wife's leave to ride out, promising to return; she is left carrying his child. He rides north out of Pelrapeire not knowing the direction holds no news of a mother fourteen months dead, but a lake, a wounded king, and a question he has been unknowingly rehearsed since infancy to fail to ask.
stops.quote: And see how my mother fareth, if weal be her lot, or woe.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: The road north from Montpellier toward the Rhône and the Jura, Parzival's traditional route
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IV
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, part I

stops.name: Lake Brumbane (Öleweiher), the fisher-king
stops.campa: After an enormous ride whose length he never afterward accounts for, Parzival comes at dusk on the nineteenth of September to a still fishing-lake in a valley he does not recognize, hemmed by rock on every side. A richly dressed man sits fishing from a boat, too sick to stand or ride, and directs the stranger to a castle he says is the only lodging for many miles. Parzival cannot see it from the water; only on climbing the far bank does Munsalvaesche appear above him, turreted, waiting, as if it had been built for this one evening alone.
suggested_refs: The Öleweiher, one of the fishponds in the valley behind the Ermitage Arlesheim, identified by Werner Greub as Wolfram's Lake Brumbane
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: Munsalvaesche (Hornikopf), the bleeding lance and the Grail procession
stops.campa: In the great round hall of Munsalvaesche, built as if turned on a lathe, four hundred knights sit at their meal beside the ailing king Anfortas, who is the fisherman from the lake. A squire runs weeping through the hall bearing a lance from whose steel point blood runs unceasing down into his sleeve, and every man there groans aloud at the sight, though none will say why. Then in solemn procession enter maidens bearing golden vessels, silver knives, candles, and last a maiden crowned above the rest carrying on green silk the thing men call the Grail, root and flower of Paradise, which alone feeds the entire hall.
stops.quote: A squire sprang swift thro' the doorway, and a lance in his hand he bore... from the point did the blood run fast adown to the hand of the holder till 'twas lost in his sleeve at last... and then thro' the lofty palace was weeping and wailing sore.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: Hornikopf hill behind the Ermitage Arlesheim, identified by Werner Greub as the site of Munsalvaesche
Manuscript illuminations of the Grail procession, e.g. Cgm 19, Bavarian State Library, Munich
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: Munsalvaesche, the silence and the sword
stops.campa: Watching the wonders of the hall and his grieving host, Parzival remembers only that Gurnemanz forbade him to ask too freely, and reasons that if he simply waits, someone will explain unasked how it stands here with this folk. Anfortas, in silent thanks that this stranger has not shamed him, presses into his hands a fine sword he can no longer wield himself. Parzival's fingers close on the hilt, the very moment, Wolfram says, when his silence might still have been broken; he says nothing. The Grail is borne out again. The feast ends. He is shown to bed unquestioned and unquestioning.
stops.quote: And he thought, 'Gurnemanz he bade me, in truth, without thought of guile, to withhold my lips from question. If here I abide awhile, methinks it will then befall me, as aforetime in Graharz land, they will tell me, without my question, how here with this folk it stands.'
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: Hornikopf hill, the Grail Castle site
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V

stops.name: Munsalvaesche, the empty castle at dawn
stops.campa: He wakes to a castle stripped of every soul, his armor set ready by unseen hands, his horse saddled and waiting in an empty courtyard hung with silence where four hundred knights supped the night before. As he rides out, the drawbridge is hauled up so sharply behind him that his horse's hindquarters are nearly caught, and a voice curses him from a window, sun of the goose, for a fool who let his chance walk past him unspoken. He rides into the forest not yet understanding what door has just been shut, or that it will take him six years to find its hinge again.
suggested_refs: Hornikopf hill, traditional site of the Grail Castle's threshold
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

segments.name: The Round Table Camp on the Birs

stops.name: South foot of Birseck, Sigune weeping a second time
stops.campa: Riding down from the castle hill he cannot find again by looking back, Parzival comes on Sigune once more, seated now aloft in a linden tree with dead Schionatulander embalmed between her white arms, her brown hair shorn away for grief. She asks eagerly whether he asked the question at Munsalvaesche, the question that would have healed her uncle Anfortas and crowned him king of the Grail. He answers that he asked nothing. She curses him outright, dishonored and accursed, and will not speak to him again; he rides from her more wretched than any battle has left him.
stops.quote: Then he quoth, 'Nay, I asked no question!' 'Alas!' cried the mournful maid, 'that ever mine eyes have seen thee, who to question wast sore afraid... Thou hast seen the knives of silver, thou the bleeding spear hast seen. Alas! wherefore hast thou sought me? Dishonoured, accurst art thou.'
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: The south foot of the Birseck castle hill at the Ermitage Arlesheim, Werner Greub's site for the second Sigune scene
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: Orilus Rock and the grotto of Proserpina, Jeschute vindicated
stops.campa: At the northern rock wall that marks the border of Soltane Forest, Parzival meets Jeschute again, still riding in the torn and shamed state Orilus imposed on her for the theft of a kiss she never invited. Duke Orilus, coming on them, attacks the stranger in fury, and this time Parzival unhorses him outright, then does what he could not do at Bromhübel: swears in a nearby cave, the grotto later called Trevrizent's, that Jeschute is and has always been innocent. Orilus, humbled, is reconciled to his wife. From the grotto's keeper Parzival takes up the spear of the knight Taurian to replace the one broken in the fight.
suggested_refs: The Proserpina Grotto (Proserpinagrotte) in the Ermitage Arlesheim, identified by Werner Greub with Trevrizent's cave
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: Stollenrain, the three drops of blood in the snow
stops.campa: A hot day turns suddenly bitter overnight; snow falls thick over the ground between Arlesheim and Dornachbrugg. At dawn a falcon of King Arthur's, hunting wild geese, strikes one down; three drops of its blood fall glowing on the white snow at Stollenrain. Parzival, riding by, is transfixed at the sight: the red on white calls up his wife Condwiramurs's face so exactly that he falls into a waking trance, lance couched but unmoving, oblivious to the world, until a passing knight of Arthur's nearby camp spots the strange, motionless Red Knight and rides to report the wonder.
stops.quote: He thought, 'Say what hand hath painted these colours that here I see? Kondwiramur, I think well, these tints sure shall liken thee!'
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: Stollenrain, Arlesheim, between the village and Dornachbrugg, identified by Werner Greub as the site of the blood-drops
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: The Round Table camp on the Plimizoel (the Birs)
stops.campa: Arthur's whole court is camped along the river Wolfram calls the Plimizoel, the Birs, from Dornachbrugg to Münchenstein, tents pitched for a Round Table held in the field. Two knights ride out to challenge the entranced Red Knight and are unhorsed without his ever quite waking, until Gawain, gentler than the rest, approaches on foot, throws a silk cloth over the blood-drops to break the trance, and leads the bewildered Parzival back to camp as a guest. There, before Arthur and Guinevere, he is at last named a companion of the Round Table, the honor he set out from Soltane a year and a half before to win.
suggested_refs: The traditional Round Table encampment site at Gstadbrunnen on the Birs, per Werner Greub
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: The Round Table camp, Cundrie's curse and the renunciation of God
stops.campa: The feast is barely begun when Cundrie the sorceress rides into camp, hideous and learned, and curses Parzival before the whole Round Table by name: he sat beside the Grail king's suffering and never asked the healing word, and every honor just given him is void. She calls the knights instead to rescue the four queens held in Klingsor's enchanted Schastel Marveil, and rides off toward it. Parzival, shattered, turns to Gawain and disowns the God he has served since infancy, swearing to seek Him no more, then rides alone from the camp that welcomed him only hours before, into six years of wandering.
stops.quote: Woe is me! Who is He, this mighty God? Had He power, then methinks our portion had ne'er been this shame abhorred! Small power shall be His! I served Him from the day I first knew His grace, henceforth I renounce His service; doth He hate me, His hate I'll face!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Parzival to Gawain
suggested_refs: The Round Table camp on the Birs, where the curse of Cundrie is traditionally placed
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12 and ch. 13

stops.name: Bearosche (Besançon), fighting on the wrong side
stops.campa: Within weeks of riding from the Birs, Parzival, still unknown by his blazon, finds himself before the walled, river-looped town of Bearosche, where Gawain has ridden to defend the townspeople against the besieging army of Meljanz. Parzival takes the field on the opposing side without recognizing his own new companion of the Round Table across the melee, one more proof that the God he has renounced has left him wandering blind even among friends. Neither man learns until much later how close their spears came that autumn under the walls of a town neither will remember naming the other.
suggested_refs: The citadel and river-loop of Besançon on the Doubs, identified by Werner Greub as Bearosche from its unmistakable Jura topography
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VII
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 11

stops.name: Schampfanzun (Champagnole), Vergulaht sent to the Grail quest
stops.campa: At Champagnole, seat of young King Vergulaht above the drained bed of an ancient Jura lake, Parzival defeats his host in single combat over an old grievance and, sparing him as he spared Kingrun and Clamide before, commits him instead to ride in search of the Grail he himself has lost. Neither man yet knows they share a grandfather, Gandin, or that this half-recognized cousin will later cross Parzival's road again through Kahenis of Punt. Parzival rides on, ignorant that Gawain will pass through this same town within days looking for the very same king.
suggested_refs: Mont Rivel above Champagnole, ruins of the castle Werner Greub proposes as Wolfram's Monte Rybele, Vergulaht's seat
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VIII
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 11

stops.name: The fountain of Lac, at the source of the Larg
stops.campa: Four years and more of tournaments and joyless victories have cracked the sword Anfortas gave him at Munsalvaesche, the one weapon left of that whole ruined night. He remembers, at last, Sigune's old counsel, that the blade came from Trebuchet's forge and can be mended only at the spring called Lac, where a stream named Karnant rises among the Sundgau hills. He finds the source, presses the broken halves together in the running water, and draws out a sword whole and brighter than before, as if the years themselves could be rejoined as cleanly, though his own wound will need a harder cure.
stops.quote: The sword will withstand the first blow, at the next it will break in twain... Lac is the name of that fountain. If unsplintered shall be the blade, then press thou its halves together, from the waters shall it be made.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Sigune's instruction, fulfilled here
suggested_refs: The source of the Largue (Larg) river at the foot of the Glaserberg near Oberlarg, above Levoncourt in the Sundgau, proposed by Werner Greub as Wolfram's Brunnen Lac
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IX
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: Sigune's cell, the third meeting
stops.campa: On a Saturday in March, Parzival rides again between the two rock gates of Terre de salvaesche, still hunting the Grail Castle he cannot relocate on his own, and finds Sigune's cell for a third time. Six years have not softened her grief; her cousin's corpse still lies embalmed across her lap. But her rage at Parzival has cooled into pity, and she tells him plainly that Cundrie was here only a little before, that her mule stands always by the rock port where the waterfall gushes, and sends him after her tracks toward Munsalvaesche one more time.
suggested_refs: Sigune's cell above the rock arch, the Ermitage Arlesheim
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IX
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: The Liten, the Templar's spear and the lost horse
stops.campa: Following Cundrie's mule-track up the rocky slope called the Liten, a crossroads Wolfram likens to a spider's web where a wrong turn is easily made, Parzival comes within sight of Munsalvaesche's outer line at last, only to be challenged by one of the Templeisen guarding the approach. Neither man yields; in the clash Parzival's own horse is killed under him. He mounts the Templar's instead and turns back into the forest, no closer to the door that shut on him six years before, but for the first time certain he is riding in the right country.
suggested_refs: The rocky slope east of Hornikopf hill identified by Werner Greub with Wolfram's Liten
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IX
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: Brizljan Forest in the snow, Kahenis of Punt
stops.campa: Cold returns hard over Brizljan Forest, ground white again as it was the day of the blood-drops, when Parzival meets a company of pilgrims on foot, barefoot in the frost for penance, led by the lord Kahenis of the water-buttressed town of Punt. They tell him it is nearly Good Friday and rebuke him gently for riding armed on the holiest days of the year; he answers, bitterly, that he has long since stopped counting holy days, having renounced the God whose mercy he no longer trusts. They point him, out of pure kindness he does not think he deserves, toward a hermit nearby who might ease his heart.
stops.quote: Since ever I bear Him hatred Whom they worship with lowly heart, and they look for His aid, Who ever hath turnèd His face from me.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IX, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Parzival's thought among the penitents
suggested_refs: The banks of the Birs between Angenstein and Dornach, identified by Werner Greub as Wolfram's Brizljan Forest
Porrentruy (Pruntrut), identified by Werner Greub as Wolfram's water-buttressed Punt, home of Kahenis
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IX
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 11

stops.name: Trevrizent's grotto, Good Friday: the confession
stops.campa: In the cave the pilgrims named, Parzival finds an old hermit in a hair shirt, Trevrizent, who turns out to be brother to Anfortas and to Herzeloyde both, his own uncle. Reading in his psalter the days that have vanished, the hermit tells him plainly that four years, six months, and three days have passed since a spear was lost from this grotto, the very spear Parzival took unknowing from this same cave after the Orilus fight. Parzival confesses everything: the silence at the Grail table, the years of blind roaming, the hatred he has nursed against a God he no longer prays to.
stops.quote: It was Taurian, quoth the hermit, who his spear in my care did leave... four years and a half and three days shall have passed since we lost the spear.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IX, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: The Proserpina Grotto, Ermitage Arlesheim, called also the Cave of Death and Resurrection, identified with Trevrizent's grotto
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IX
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: Trevrizent's grotto, Easter: the teaching and the going forth
stops.campa: Through Holy Week and Easter, Trevrizent unfolds to his nephew the whole hidden history he has never heard: that the Grail is a stone, not a cup, borne by angels neutral in Heaven's old war and given since to a chosen family of guardians; that Anfortas's wound is punishment for a sin of pride in love, curable only by the compassionate question Parzival once failed to ask; and that God's mercy, far from having abandoned him, has been waiting the whole six years for him to stop cursing it. On the seventh of April Parzival rides out again reconciled, no longer a fool but not yet a king.
stops.quote: Sir Knight, thou shalt put away such madness, and trust God better, for His help will He never stay.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IX, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Trevrizent to Parzival
suggested_refs: The Proserpina Grotto, Ermitage Arlesheim
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IX
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

segments.name: Whitsuntide: The Duels and the Redemption

stops.name: Joflanze (the Kembs plain), the camp of kings assembles
stops.campa: On the great sheep-plain the country calls Schofland, opposite the rock of Isteiner Klotz on the German shore, King Arthur's whole train arrives from Beaune to make good Gawain's promise of a duel with Gramoflanz over a garland won from a fatal tree. Tents rise for Arthur, for Orgeluse, for Gramoflanz's own army marching from Mülhausen; among the throng of unbadged knights drawn to any gathering of arms rides Parzival, once again unrecognized, once again about to collide with people he loves before he knows their faces in the press of tents and banners.
suggested_refs: The Rhine plain near Kembs, opposite Isteiner Klotz, identified by Werner Greub as Wolfram's Joflanze
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 13, 'Schastel Marveil'

stops.name: Mönchsberg, the duel with an unknown knight
stops.campa: On the plateau above Mülhausen, near the old Roman road and the watchtower, Parzival and a knight he has never met fight to a standstill neither can explain, matching stroke for stroke until both are near collapse and their weapons are shattered in each other's hands. Only when the fight is broken off by onlookers does it emerge, to the astonishment and joy of both, that the stranger is Gawain, the same friend who once lifted the blood-trance from him on the Birs. They embrace where moments before they meant to kill each other, and ride together into camp as brothers again.
stops.quote: But he cast from his hand his weapon, and he cried, as he wept full sore, 'Accursèd am I, and dishonoured, and all blessing from me hath flown, since my luckless hand, unwitting, so sinful a strife hath known.'
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Parzival on learning his foe is Gawain
suggested_refs: The Ferme Mönchsberg, on the plateau south of the Mülhausen watchtower, identified by Werner Greub as the duel site
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 13

stops.name: Illberg, the garland and the duel with Gramoflanz
stops.campa: At the lime tree on the Illberg above the perilous ford of the Ill, the same tree whose garland Gawain won and whose owner Gramoflanz demanded satisfaction for, Parzival takes up his friend's unfinished quarrel and fights the king of Rosche Sabins to a standstill in his place, since Gawain's own wounds and Orgeluse's grief have made a substitute necessary. Arthur, arriving with his whole camp from Bems, brokers a peace between the households before more blood is spilled over a wreath of leaves, and the field that nearly hosted a third funeral instead hosts a wedding feast for Gramoflanz and Gawain's sister Itonje.
suggested_refs: The Illberg south of Mulhouse-Dornach, identified by Werner Greub as the site of Gramoflanz's tree
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 13

stops.name: Breisacherwald, Feirefiss the black-and-white brother
stops.campa: In the great oak forest north of Istein, a magnificently armed stranger rides ashore from a fleet anchored in a closed arm of the Rhine and challenges Parzival to single combat; the two fight so evenly that the sword Parzival robbed from dead Ither breaks sheer on the heathen's helmet, God no longer willing him lord of a stolen blade, at which the stranger, rather than press it, casts his own weapon far from him, refusing to win against an unarmed knight. Only then do names come out: this is Feirefiss, the black-and-white son Gahmuret left behind, Parzival's half-brother, sailing west in search of the father neither ever really had.
stops.quote: Now I see well, thou gallant hero, thou hast no sword wherewith to fight, and the fame shall be small I win me if I fight with an unarmed knight.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Feirefiss to Parzival
suggested_refs: The Hardtwald forest between Niffer and Petit-Landau, identified by Werner Greub as Wolfram's Breisacherwald (Laeprisin)
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XV
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 13

stops.name: The Kembs plain, Cundrie's return and the call to the throne
stops.campa: The morning after the brothers' reconciliation, Cundrie the sorceress rides again into camp, this time not to curse but to kneel: the stars have turned, she says, and named Parzival at last as the destined lord of the Grail, if he will only come now, this Whitsuntide, and ask the question the years have taught him to ask. She names his young son by Condwiramurs, Kardeis, unborn when he left Pelrapeire and unknown to him until this hour, and Loherangrin, a second son, both proof his marriage bore fruit through all the wandering. Parzival chooses Feirefiss to ride with him; Cundrie leads the way.
stops.quote: Now rejoice with a humble heart, since the crown of all earthly blessings henceforward shall be thy part, for read is the mystic writing. The Grail, It doth hail thee king, and Kondwiramur, thy true wife, thou shalt to thy kingdom bring.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Cundrie to Parzival
suggested_refs: The Kembs plain, Cundrie's second appearance
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XV
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 13

stops.name: Barbigoel to Schönmatt: the ride to Munsalvaesche, and the redemption of Anfortas
stops.campa: On Whitsun Saturday the three ride through Barbigoel, Basle, over Karchobra at Münchenstein, and down by Winterhalde to Schönmatt, until Munsalvaesche rises above them from the Hornikopf as it did that first September evening. In the great round hall, before Anfortas laid dying on his litter, the lance is carried in once more, and this time Parzival, kneeling thrice in the Name of the Trinity, asks the question all Terre de salvaesche has waited a generation to hear: what aileth thee here, mine uncle? Anfortas is healed in an instant; the wound closes; the king of the Grail names his successor with his own breath.
stops.quote: What aileth thee here, mine uncle?
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XVI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), the Grail question
suggested_refs: Hornikopf hill, the Grail Castle, redemption site
Manuscript illuminations of Anfortas healed, in the major Parzival codices (e.g. Munich Cgm 19, St. Gallen Cod. 857)
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XVI
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12 and ch. 13

stops.name: Birseck, the night visit to Trevrizent
stops.campa: In the same night of the redemption, before dawn can even announce Whitsunday, Parzival rides down from Munsalvaesche with a company of Templars to the grotto at Birseck to bring Trevrizent the news his own prayers of six Good Fridays have finally answered. The hermit who once told him God's help would never fail weeps to hear it confirmed, and blesses his nephew now not as a penitent but as the Grail King he always half suspected the boy in the fool's coat would become, closing a circle that began the day the two first met in ash and hair shirt.
suggested_refs: The Proserpina Grotto, Ermitage Arlesheim, site of Trevrizent's cell
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XVI
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: Stollenrain, the dawn reunion with Kyot and Condwiramurs
stops.campa: At the place of the three blood-drops near Dornachbrugg, where six years before a fallen goose's blood on snow first showed him his wife's face, Parzival meets at dawn his uncle Kyot, who has ridden the length of France to bring Condwiramurs and their son Kardeis from Montpellier to the Grail throne, exactly as he once escorted Schoysiane to this same country a generation earlier. The reunion is wordless at first, husband and wife having parted as strangers to what either would become; Kyot, his errand done, turns back toward Montpellier to raise young Kardeis to rule there in his father's stead.
suggested_refs: Stollenrain, Arlesheim, site of both blood-drop scenes six years apart
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XVI
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, part I and ch. 12

stops.name: Fontane la salvaesche, the death of Sigune
stops.campa: Toward evening, leading his wife and son up toward Munsalvaesche, Parzival halts by the rock arch that has marked every turn of his story, and climbs with them the stairs cut into the cave to greet Sigune a last time. She is dead, still kneeling in the posture of grief she never once set down in six years, Schionatulander's embalmed body still in her lap. They open the tomb and lay her to rest beside him at last, the two lovers united in death as they never were permitted to be in life, while Condwiramurs weeps for a woman she has never met but instantly understands.
stops.quote: There, embalmed lay Schionatulander, nor long should he lie alone, for beside him they laid the maiden, who in life to him true love gave in such wise as beseemed a maiden, and they closed o'er the twain the grave.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XVI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: Sigune's cell above the rock arch, the Ermitage Arlesheim, traditional site of her burial beside Schionatulander
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XVI
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12

stops.name: Munsalvaesche, Whitsunday: Parzival crowned Grail King
stops.campa: That Whitsuntide evening the whole company of Templeisen receives Condwiramurs as their new queen with a feast at which the Grail mystery play is performed again, not to test a silent guest but to seat him as host. Parzival is enthroned where Anfortas suffered so long, Feirefiss beside him newly baptized for love of Repanse de Schoie, whom he will marry and carry east to found, the story says, a line of Christian kings in his mother's country. The fool who once knelt to armored strangers thinking them gods now sits where the Grail itself once fed four hundred, and is fed by no one's error ever again.
suggested_refs: Hornikopf hill, Munsalvaesche, the Grail Castle throne room
The Goetheanum, Dornach, built in the twentieth century on the strength of Rudolf Steiner's identification of this same valley as Grail country
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XVI
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 12
